title: Three Ships. Three Dead Indians. And a Prime Minister Who Has Not Said a Word.
excerpt: As U.S. forces fire missiles into oil tankers crewed by Indian sailors, families grieve in Deoria, unions rage, the opposition smells blood — and Modi boards a plane to Europe.
body:
Sushila Devi sat sobbing on the floor of her house in Deoria, in northern India's Uttar Pradesh, after authorities told her that her husband was one of three sailors killed when the U.S. military fired precision munitions into the engine room of an oil tanker off Oman.

"If he had told us about the dangers, I would have called him back," she cried, as women from the family gathered around her. "The government should not allow people to go there."

Her husband, Shivanand Chaurasia, was the sole earner in a family with two young children. He was among 24 Indian mariners aboard the Palau-flagged tanker Settebello when it was struck on Tuesday. The U.S. military's Central Command said the crew "repeatedly failed to comply with directions from American forces" during an ongoing blockade targeting Iranian oil shipments.

Three days. Three ships. Three dead Indians. And a political storm that is now threatening to overshadow Prime Minister Narendra Modi's trip to Europe, where he departs Saturday for a G7 summit where he is expected to sit across from Donald Trump for the first time since last year's India-Pakistan conflict.

**The toll is mounting fast.** On June 8, U.S. forces disabled the Palau-flagged tanker Marivex, carrying 24 Indian seafarers — all rescued. On June 10, the Settebello was struck, killing three. On June 12, Hellfire missiles hit the Guinea-Bissau-flagged Jalveer, carrying 20 Indian crew who were reported safe. As of Thursday, U.S. CENTCOM has disabled nine ships in the Gulf and redirected 135 others, with Indian nationals comprising the bulk of the merchant crews caught in the crossfire.

India's foreign ministry summoned the U.S. chargé d'affaires, Jason Meeks, for a second time in three days — a rare diplomatic escalation. "Such actions are unacceptable and undermine the safety, security and stability of international maritime commerce," the ministry said.

But the opposition wants far more than diplomatic protests.

**Rahul Gandhi launched a direct attack on Modi on Friday**, demanding that the prime minister personally confront Washington. "Three Indians have been killed in U.S. attacks on three ships in international waters within three days," Gandhi wrote on social media. "When any foreign power murders an Indian, the Prime Minister has to speak up. A compromised PM cannot protect the sons of Mother India because he lacks either the courage or the strength to confront those who took their lives."

The Congress party accused the government's policies of having "emboldened external powers to act against Indian interests with impunity." The Aam Aadmi Party urged Modi to take up the matter directly with Trump. India's Centre of Indian Trade Unions demanded that the government "speak — loudly and firmly." The Forward Seamen's Union of India called it a "gruesome attack."

"I have only one demand: that my son's remains be brought back," said Rajesh Sharma, the father of one of the dead seafarers. "I want to know what happened in his last moments. Was he given any rescue assistance?"

**India is one of the world's largest suppliers of merchant marine labour**, with more than 300,000 seafarers working on ships globally — making it the second-largest source of commercial sailors behind the Philippines. Many work on foreign-flagged vessels in the volatile Gulf region, leaving them exposed when geopolitical tensions escalate. Maritime unions warn that repeated attacks could deter workers from taking up seafaring jobs, worsening an industry already facing labour shortages.

Political scientist Kanti Bajpai, a visiting senior fellow at India's Centre for Social and Economic Progress, said the deaths have "already become an irritant in a wobbling relationship" between Delhi and Washington. Further casualties and "the venting of public outrage at home" could make it harder for the Modi government to contain the fallout, he warned.

Modi has not commented publicly on the deaths. He departs for Nice on Saturday, then travels to Slovakia before reaching Evian-les-Bains for the G7 summit on June 16. Whether the seafarer crisis will be raised formally with Trump remains unclear — but the political pressure to do so is building by the hour.

*Sources: Reuters, CNN, Swadesi, LatestLY, New York Post*
